title: The Rose Bowl That Changed the South
dek: Alabama wasn't the Rose Bowl's first choice. Down 12–0 at halftime in Pasadena, the Crimson Tide gave the whole South something to brag about.
body: In 1925, Southern football was an afterthought to the rest of the country. Wallace Wade's Alabama team went unbeaten that fall and gave up just one touchdown all season, but the Rose Bowl still went looking elsewhere for an opponent. Several schools turned the invitation down before the committee settled on Alabama, which had never played in a bowl game.
## A long way from home

Getting there was its own ordeal. Wade told his players they'd give up Christmas at home, practice for weeks longer than usual and ride a train for days across the country. Along the route, crowds and bands turned out at the stations to see them off. Nobody had said it out loud yet, but they weren't just representing Alabama anymore.
## Twelve down

Washington looked like the better team for a half. Its star, George Wilson, ran the Huskies down the field, and they led 12–0 at the break. Both of their extra points had missed, which nobody thought much about at the time.

Then Alabama found its footing in the third quarter and scored three touchdowns in less than seven minutes. Pooley Hubert ran one in from the 1. Grant Gillis hit Johnny Mack Brown for a 59-yard touchdown. Hubert threw 30 yards to Brown for another. The last extra point missed, so Alabama led 20–12.

Wilson answered with a 27-yard touchdown pass late, and this time Washington made the kick. That left the Huskies one point short, and it stayed that way. In the closing seconds, Brown made the tackle that ended Washington's last chance. He was named the game's most valuable player.
## What it meant

The win gave Alabama its first national championship and its first perfect season. Back home it meant far more than that. Tuscaloosa held a parade for the team that ended on the Quad. People still call it the game that changed the South.

The Rose Bowl kept coming back for more. Southern teams played in 13 of the next 20 Rose Bowls, and Alabama made more of those trips than anyone. Brown went on to a long career as a Hollywood cowboy star, but Alabama fans remember him for that afternoon in Pasadena.

title: Frank Thomas and the Notre Dame Box
dek: Between Wallace Wade and Bear Bryant came a Notre Dame quarterback who won two national titles, two Rose Bowls and 115 games, and gets remembered least of the three.
body: When Wallace Wade decided to leave Alabama after the 1930 season, he picked his own successor. His choice was Frank Thomas, a young coach who had played quarterback at Notre Dame for Knute Rockne in the early 1920s and roomed with George Gipp.
## A new offense

Thomas did not just take over Wade's team, he changed how it played. He retired the single-wing offense Alabama had won with and installed the Notre Dame Box, the shifting formation he learned under Rockne. His first team went 9–1.
## The 1934 team

Three years later Thomas had one of the best teams in the country. The 1934 Crimson Tide went 10–0, beat Stanford 29–13 in the Rose Bowl and was named national champion. One of its ends was an Arkansas kid named Paul Bryant, who was known as "the other end" to the more famous Don Hutson. After his playing days, Bryant joined Thomas's staff as an assistant.
Thomas kept winning. Alabama went back to Pasadena after the 1937 season. In 1941 the Tide won another national title. After the 1945 season, an unbeaten Alabama team beat USC 34–14 in the Rose Bowl.
## Coaching from a trailer

By then, Thomas's health was failing. Heart trouble left him unable to stand on the practice field for long, and in his last years he ran practice from a trailer at the edge of the field. He stepped down after the 1946 season and stayed on as athletic director. He died in Tuscaloosa in 1954, at 55.
## Why he's forgotten

His Alabama record was 115–24–7 over 16 seasons. That's two national championships, two Rose Bowl wins and a College Football Hall of Fame induction in 1951. The problem is timing. He followed the coach who put Alabama on the map, and his best-known player became the most famous coach in the sport. Wade and Bryant cast long shadows, and Thomas stood right between them.

title: Mama Called
dek: Bear Bryant had a winner at Texas A&M. Alabama had won four games in three years. Here's why he came home anyway.
body: By the end of 1957, Paul Bryant was one of the hottest coaches in the country. He had won an SEC title at Kentucky. At Texas A&M he had survived the brutal 1954 camp at Junction, Texas, where most of the roster quit and the survivors went 1–9, and turned those players into a Southwest Conference champion by 1956.
Alabama, meanwhile, was in the worst stretch of its history. From 1955 through 1957 the Crimson Tide won four games total.
## The answer

Bryant had played at Alabama in the 1930s, an end on Frank Thomas's 1934 national championship team, and he had coached there as an assistant afterward. When his alma mater asked him to come back, he gave the explanation people still quote. Mama called, he said. He meant his alma mater, and everybody understood.
## Starting over

The turnaround was not instant. His first Alabama game, in Mobile in September 1958, was a 13–3 loss to LSU. But that first team finished 5–4–1, more wins than the three previous seasons combined. In 1961, his fourth season, Alabama won the national championship.
## Twenty-five years

He stayed for 25 seasons. His Alabama teams went 232–46–9, won six national championships and 13 SEC titles, and went to 24 straight bowl games. His last game was a 21–15 win over Illinois in the Liberty Bowl in December 1982. A month later, on Jan. 26, 1983, he died of a heart attack in Tuscaloosa at 69.
Most coaches leave a good job for a better one. Bryant left a winning program for a losing one because it was home, and Alabama has measured every coach since against what happened next.

title: The Goal Line Stand
dek: No. 1 Penn State had first down at the Alabama 19 and seven minutes to tie the Sugar Bowl. Four downs later, it was still a foot short.
body: The 1979 Sugar Bowl was the game the whole country wanted: No. 1 Penn State against No. 2 Alabama, with the national championship on the line in New Orleans.
## Seven points of separation

Alabama struck right before halftime. With eight seconds left in the second quarter, Jeff Rutledge threw 30 yards to Bruce Bolton for a touchdown and a 7–0 lead. The teams traded touchdowns in the third quarter, with Major Ogilvie scoring for Alabama behind a block from tight end Rick Neal, and it was 14–7 going into the fourth.
Then Alabama fumbled. Penn State's Joe Lally fell on it at the Alabama 19 with 7:57 left, and the best team in the country was 19 yards from tying the game.
## Down to inches

Matt Suhey ran 11 yards to the 8. Mike Guman got two more to the 6. On second down, Chuck Fusina threw to Scott Fitzkee near the goal line, and cornerback Don McNeal drove him out of bounds about two feet short.
On third down, Penn State gave it to Suhey up the middle. Linebacker Rich Wingo met him, with David Hannah and safety Murray Legg piling in. Still short.
## Fourth and inches

During the timeout, Alabama's Marty Lyons told Fusina he'd better throw it. Penn State didn't. Guman went up and over the pile, and linebacker Barry Krauss met him in midair, helmet to helmet. Guman didn't get in.

Krauss was named the game's most valuable player, and he's still the only linebacker to win that award. Alabama finished No. 1 in the AP poll, and Bear Bryant had his fifth national championship. The UPI coaches' poll went with USC, so the title was split, but in Alabama nobody remembers that part. They remember the stand.
sources: Remembering the 1979 Goal Line Stand (Allstate Sugar Bowl)
Crimson Tide Top 10 Sugar Bowls: No. 1, 1979 Alabama vs. Penn State (Sports Illustrated)

dek: Bear Bryant needed one more win to pass Amos Alonzo Stagg as the winningest coach in college football. The schedule handed him Auburn.
body: For decades, the record for wins by a major college football coach belonged to Amos Alonzo Stagg, who coached from the 1890s into the 1940s. In November 1981, Bear Bryant had 314. One more would make him the winningest coach in the history of the sport.
The next game on the schedule was Auburn, at Legion Field in Birmingham, on national television.
## The student

Auburn had a first-year coach that season, Pat Dye. He knew Bryant well, having spent nine years on his staff at Alabama as a linebackers coach, and his Tigers came in at 5–4. Bryant's Alabama team was ranked No. 4, but nobody expected Auburn to hand over the record.
## Back and forth

They didn't. Gary Hollingsworth ran for Alabama's first touchdown, and Auburn answered to tie it 7–7 at halftime. Jesse Bendross caught a touchdown pass from Ken Coley to put Alabama up 14–7. Auburn tied it again and then went ahead 17–14 on a field goal.

Alabama didn't flinch. Walter Lewis hit Bendross for his second touchdown catch of the day to retake the lead at 21–17, and Linnie Patrick ran for another score to make it 28–17. The defense shut Auburn out from there.
## The record

That was win No. 315, more than anyone had won before. Alabama finished the regular season 9–1–1 and shared the SEC title with Georgia. Bryant coached one more season, retired after the 1982 Liberty Bowl with 323 wins, and died a month later.
Of all the places to break the record, it happened in the Iron Bowl, against a coach he had trained. The fact that it came against Auburn just makes it sweeter.

title: The Wishbone Switch
dek: After two mediocre seasons, people said the game had passed Bear Bryant by. He spent the summer of 1971 learning a new offense in secret.
body: After three national titles in the 1960s, Alabama slipped. The Tide went 6–5 in 1969 and 6–5–1 in 1970, and USC came to Birmingham in 1970 and won 42–21. For the first time, people wondered out loud whether Bear Bryant had lost his touch.
## Summer school in Texas

Bryant's answer was to go back to school. In the summer of 1971 he went to Austin to see his friend Darrell Royal, whose Texas teams had been winning with a new option offense called the wishbone. Royal walked him through it. Alabama didn't have a classic passing quarterback, and the wishbone didn't need one.
## Keep it quiet

Bryant made the switch and swore everyone to secrecy. He had campus security and Tuscaloosa police check the apartments that overlooked practice and chase away anyone watching from the rooftops. Local reporters who figured it out were warned not to print it.
## The reveal

The secret came out on Sept. 10, 1971, at the Los Angeles Coliseum. The same USC team that had embarrassed Alabama a year earlier was heavily favored again. Alabama lined up in the wishbone, scored two quick touchdowns and held on to win 17–10.
That team, led by running back Johnny Musso, went 11–0 in the regular season, beat an unbeaten Auburn team 31–7, and lost only in the Orange Bowl to Nebraska.
## A decade of wins
Then the wishbone took off. From 1971 through 1979, Alabama went 97–11. It won the SEC title eight times in the decade and claimed national championships in 1973, 1978 and 1979.
Bryant was in his late 50s and had already won three national titles. He could have kept doing what he knew. Instead he went to Texas, learned something new, and won three more.
sources: 1971 Alabama vs. USC and the Wishbone Surprise (Sports Illustrated)

title: Stallings and the Miami Upset
dek: Miami had won 29 straight, had the Heisman winner and was favored by eight. Alabama's defense had other ideas.
body: The 1993 Sugar Bowl matched No. 1 Miami against No. 2 Alabama for the national championship. Miami hadn't lost in 29 games. Its quarterback, Gino Torretta, had just won the Heisman Trophy. Oddsmakers made the Hurricanes eight-point favorites, and most of the country assumed the title was theirs.
Gene Stallings's Alabama team was 12–0 and built around a defense that didn't care what anybody thought.
## Eleven on the line

Alabama spent the night confusing Torretta. At one point the Tide lined up all 11 defenders on the line of scrimmage and dared him to figure it out. He threw three interceptions, after throwing only four all season.
One of them went to George Teague, who returned it 31 yards for a touchdown.
## The Strip

Then came the play Alabama fans still talk about. Miami receiver Lamar Thomas caught a long pass and was running free toward the end zone. Teague chased him down from behind and ripped the ball out of his hands.

It didn't count. Alabama had been offside on the play, so it came back. But if Teague hadn't caught Thomas, Miami would have scored and declined the penalty. The strip saved a touchdown, even though it never shows up in the box score.
## Running it down their throats

Alabama's offense did the rest on the ground. The Tide ran for 267 yards. Derrick Lassic scored twice and was named the game's most valuable player. Michael Proctor added two field goals, and Sherman Williams ran for another touchdown.
Final: Alabama 34, Miami 13. The Tide finished 13–0 with the program's 12th national title, its first since 1979 and the first since Bear Bryant's death.

title: The Process Begins
dek: Nick Saban's first Alabama team lost four straight in November, including one to Louisiana-Monroe at home. Two years later, Alabama was national champion.
body: On Jan. 3, 2007, Alabama announced that it had hired Nick Saban away from the Miami Dolphins. He had already won a national championship at LSU. Alabama hadn't won one since 1992.
## A rough first fall

The first season showed how far the program had to go. Alabama started well enough, but November was a disaster. The Tide lost to LSU, then Mississippi State. Then, on Nov. 17 at Bryant-Denny Stadium, it lost 21–14 to Louisiana-Monroe, a Sun Belt team that was supposed to be a tune-up. Alabama lost its regular-season finale too, making four losses in a row.

Saban later called the Louisiana-Monroe game the most humiliating loss of his time at Alabama. He didn't blow up the plan, though. He talked about doing things the right way every day, regardless of the scoreboard. People started calling it the Process.

Alabama beat Colorado 30–24 in the Independence Bowl in Shreveport to finish 7–6 on the field. The NCAA later vacated five of those wins for a textbook violation, so the official record looks even worse.
## The turn

Then things turned. In 2008, Alabama opened by beating Clemson 34–10 in Atlanta and went 12–0 in the regular season. It lost the SEC Championship Game to Florida and the Sugar Bowl to Utah, but it was clear the program had turned the corner.
In 2009, Alabama went 14–0, avenged the Florida loss 32–13 in Atlanta, and beat Texas 37–21 in Pasadena for the national championship.
## What came next
That was title No. 1 for Saban at Alabama. Five more followed in 2011, 2012, 2015, 2017 and 2020. Most dynasties have a starting point, and Saban's started with a 21–14 loss to Louisiana-Monroe.
sources: Nick Saban opens up about 'the most humiliating defeat' (Sportskeeda)

title: The Game of the Century Rematch
dek: LSU beat Alabama 9–6 in the Game of the Century. Two months later, LSU didn't score at all.
body: On Nov. 5, 2011, No. 1 LSU visited No. 2 Alabama in a game billed as the Game of the Century. Neither team scored a touchdown. Alabama missed four field goals, and LSU's Drew Alleman won it 9–6 in overtime with a 25-yarder.

That should have been the end of Alabama's title hopes. Instead, upsets elsewhere moved the 11–1 Tide up to No. 2 in the final BCS standings. Plenty of people thought Oklahoma State deserved the spot. Alabama got it anyway, and the rematch was set for New Orleans.
## The kicker's redemption

Jeremy Shelley had been part of Alabama's kicking misery in November. In the rematch he made five field goals, from 23, 34, 41, 35 and 44 yards, a bowl record. The 44-yarder was the longest of his career, and he scored 15 of Alabama's 21 points.
## LSU couldn't move

Alabama's defense was even better. LSU managed one first down in the first half and didn't reach midfield until the fourth quarter. When it finally did, Dont'a Hightower sacked the quarterback and forced a fumble.
A few plays later, Trent Richardson broke a 34-yard touchdown run with 6:15 left, the only touchdown either team scored in eight quarters against each other that season.
LSU finished with 92 total yards and five first downs. Alabama's defense had 11 tackles for loss, four sacks and an interception.
## The first of its kind
Alabama 21, LSU 0. It was the first shutout in any BCS bowl game. AJ McCarron, who completed 23 of 34 passes for 234 yards, was named offensive MVP, and Courtney Upshaw won the defensive award.
It was Alabama's 14th national championship and Saban's second in Tuscaloosa. LSU had won the first game. Alabama won the one that counted.
sources: Crimson Tide wins 14th national championship, 21–0, over LSU (Alabama Athletics)
LSU beats Bama in battle of field goals, 9–6 in OT (Deseret News / AP)

title: 2nd and 26
dek: Down 13–0 at halftime of the national championship, Nick Saban turned to a freshman quarterback who had barely played. Then came one throw in overtime.
body: The 2018 national championship game was in Atlanta, at Georgia's back door, and for a half it belonged to Georgia. The Bulldogs' defense kept Alabama off the scoreboard, and they led 13–0 at halftime.
## The switch
Nick Saban made a decision almost no coach would make in a title game. He pulled his starter, Jalen Hurts, and sent in Tua Tagovailoa, a true freshman who had spent the season as the backup.

Tagovailoa played like he'd been there all along. Alabama scored 20 points in the second half to tie the game. With the clock running out in regulation, Alabama lined up for a 36-yard field goal to win it. Andy Pappanastos missed, and the game went to overtime.
## The worst possible start
Georgia got the ball first in overtime and Rodrigo Blankenship made a 51-yard field goal. Alabama needed only a field goal to keep playing.
On the first snap, Tagovailoa held the ball too long and was sacked for a 16-yard loss. That made it second down and 26 from the Georgia 41, which pushed Alabama nearly out of field goal range.
## One throw
On the next play, Tagovailoa threw deep to another freshman, DeVonta Smith, for a 41-yard touchdown. Alabama won 26–23, and the game ended right there.
Tagovailoa threw three touchdown passes and was named offensive player of the game. Da'Ron Payne won the defensive award. It was Saban's sixth national title and Alabama's fifth in nine seasons.
Three years later, Smith won the Heisman Trophy. But no catch he ever made topped that one, from a freshman quarterback on 2nd and 26.
sources: 2018 CFP National Championship recap (College Football Playoff)
Walk-off: Alabama beats Georgia in OT for national title (AP via The Gazette)

title: Four Heismans
dek: For 74 years Alabama won titles without a Heisman Trophy. Then it won four in 13 seasons: a running back, a bigger running back, a receiver and a quarterback.
body: Alabama won a dozen national championships before it ever had a Heisman Trophy winner. Plenty of great players came close. None of them won it. Then, under Nick Saban, the Tide won four in 13 seasons, and each one was a different kind of player.
## Mark Ingram, 2009

The first one came down to the wire. Ingram, a sophomore running back, beat Stanford's Toby Gerhart by 28 points, 1,304 to 1,276. That was the closest vote in the history of the award. Alabama went on to finish 14–0 and win the national title.
## Derrick Henry, 2015

Henry was the workhorse of a title team. By the time the votes came in, he had 1,986 rushing yards, which broke Herschel Walker's SEC single-season record, and 23 rushing touchdowns, which tied the league record. He beat Christian McCaffrey by 293 points. A month later, Alabama beat Clemson 45–40 for the national championship.
## DeVonta Smith, 2020

The freshman who caught the 2nd-and-26 touchdown in 2018 became the first wide receiver to win the Heisman since Michigan's Desmond Howard in 1991. Smith finished the season with 117 catches for 1,856 yards and 23 touchdowns. Alabama went 13–0 and won the title.
## Bryce Young, 2021

The next year, Alabama won it again. Young, a sophomore, became the first Alabama quarterback to win the Heisman. When he won, he had thrown for 4,322 yards and 43 touchdowns with just four interceptions.
## One trophy case

Before 2009 the Heisman was the one big trophy Alabama didn't have. Now it has four, and they include one of the closest votes ever, a broken SEC rushing record, the first receiver to win in nearly 30 years and the program's first quarterback winner.
sources: Mark Ingram delivers Alabama its first Heisman (AP via Record-Courier)
Alabama running back Derrick Henry wins Heisman Trophy (CBS News / AP)
Bryce Young wins 2021 Heisman Memorial Trophy (Alabama Athletics)

title: The Rocky Block
dek: Unbeaten Alabama couldn't find the end zone, Tennessee had the last kick, and a 354-pound nose tackle got a hand on it.
body: Alabama hosted Tennessee in October 2009 at 7–0 and near the top of every poll. Tennessee came in at 3–3 in Lane Kiffin's first and only season in Knoxville. On paper it was a mismatch. For four quarters at Bryant-Denny Stadium, it never played like one.
## Four kicks and no touchdowns

Alabama moved the ball between the 20s all afternoon and stalled every time it got close. Leigh Tiffin carried the offense: field goals of 38, 50 and 22 yards before halftime, and a 49-yarder with 6:31 left that made it 12–3. Greg McElroy threw for 120 yards and no touchdowns. Mark Ingram ran for 99.

The defense did the rest. Tennessee kicked one short field goal in the second quarter and missed from 47 as the half ran out. With a little over ten minutes to play, Daniel Lincoln lined up a 43-yarder, and Terrence Cody blocked it. That was the first one. Alabama's defense hadn't given up a touchdown in more than eleven quarters, and with six minutes left it looked like that streak would last another week.
## Four minutes of trouble

Then it came apart. Inside the last four minutes, Eric Berry knocked the ball loose from Ingram at the Alabama 43, and Tennessee recovered. Jonathan Crompton finished the drive with an 11-yard touchdown pass to Gerald Jones with 1:19 left. The extra point made it 12–10.

Out of timeouts, Tennessee tried an onside kick and got it back at its own 41. Crompton hit Jones for 14 yards, then found tight end Luke Stocker for 23 more to the Alabama 27. Two plays later the Vols sent Lincoln back out for a 44-yard try to win it. Alabama called timeout with four seconds on the clock.
## Mount Cody

Cody was 6-foot-5 and about 354 pounds, and teammates called him Mount Cody. On the snap he shoved past Tennessee's left guard and raised his left arm. He didn't need to jump. Lincoln's kick hit his hand and skidded away sideways, and Alabama fell on it at its own 28 as the clock hit zero.

It was Cody's second blocked field goal of the fourth quarter, and it was the difference between 8–0 and a season-wrecking loss. Alabama fans gave it a name that twists Tennessee's own fight song: the Rocky Block. Cody and Tiffin were both named SEC players of the week.
## What it saved

Nobody knew it yet, but Cody had saved a perfect season. Alabama didn't lose again. It beat Florida 32–13 for the SEC title, beat Texas 37–21 in Pasadena for the program's 13th national championship, and finished 14–0, Nick Saban's first title in Tuscaloosa. Ingram, whose fumble nearly cost Alabama the Tennessee game, won the Heisman Trophy that December.
Of all the wins in that title run, none came closer to being a loss.
sources: Tennessee vs. Alabama box score, Oct. 24, 2009 (Tennessee Athletics)
Cody, Tiffin named SEC Players of the Week (Alabama Athletics)
The last time Alabama-Tennessee mattered (Sports Illustrated)
